findings.title: "Tick as transaction" atomicity is asserted but has no implementing mechanism
findings.description: The "Tick as transaction" principle promises each tick is "discrete, atomic: read current state, compute next state, commit" and that "between ticks, the world is consistent and queryable." Nothing in the design implements a staging/commit. Slice 303 (Behavior Engine Integration) has `engine.tick(state=entity_manager.state, ...)` mutate canonical state **in place**, and the document's own step 4 ("Apply the updated entity state as the new canonical state") describes no shadow buffer. A mid-tick exception in a force, query, or integration call therefore leaves positions partially updated and velocities stale — a torn state that is exactly what the principle rules out. No rollback, double-buffering, or validation (e.g., NaN check) is specified. Either define read/compute/commit with rollback on error, or drop the atomicity claim and document that a failed tick leaves partial state.

findings.title: Tick/asyncio coexistence fails under overrun — the event loop can be starved exactly when it matters
findings.description: "Tick loop and asyncio coexistence" says the boundary is "run the tick synchronously, then yield to the async event loop for I/O between ticks," asserting I/O is not starved. But the tick body wired in slice 303 is a fully synchronous `sim.step()` with no await point, and slice 301 skips `asyncio.sleep()` entirely when `remaining < 0`. Under sustained overruns — precisely when CPU-bound NumPy ticks are heavy — there is no suspension anywhere: `await tick_body()` on a coroutine that never awaits does not yield, and the sleep is skipped. WebSocket handlers starve and clients go unserved, contradicting the "Observable by default" goal. The "offload the tick to a thread or process (NumPy releases the GIL)" upgrade path also conflates the two: a process has its own GIL and gains nothing from NumPy's GIL release, and it would reintroduce the IPC/state-copying that "single-process simplicity" forbids. Need an unconditional yield (e.g., `await asyncio.sleep(0)` every tick) and a thread-based, not process-based, offload story with explicit state ownership.

findings.title: The one-way server-push protocol cannot carry the per-client culling the design depends on
findings.description: "State flows outward — Nothing flows back from clients into simulation state in v1" (## Design Goals) and the slice-305 "server-push only" protocol conflict with the "Network egress is the second scaling wall" paragraph and slice 309, which require "per-client spatial culling" where "each client declares a viewport or region of interest" and receives only what is "within their view frustum." A frustum/ROI is client→server data, and v1 defines no channel for it, yet culling is the stated answer to the 120 MB/s egress problem. The claim that the protocol "should not preclude adding them later" is asserted with no mechanism. Either define a minimal client→server ROI/subscription message as an explicit exception to the push-only rule and build it into the protocol slice (306) so it is not retrofitted, or defer culling and accept full-snapshot egress in v1.
